aspects.says: The chosen overload is written into the caller's class file, so a new overload reaches a caller only when it is recompiled.
basis: section:Design Note: Why Overloads Are Bound at Compile Time
aspects.reason: it shows only when a caller compiled against one version of a library runs against another; a graded run compiles the practice once

aspects.says: A boxed number fits an Object overload by subtyping in the first phase, so it never unboxes to reach a primitive overload.
basis: section:Widening First, Then Boxing, Then Varargs: the First Phase That Fits Wins

aspects.says: Removing an int from a collection keyed by Long boxes it to an Integer, which never equals a Long, so nothing is removed.
basis: section:On a List of Integers, remove(int) Takes an Index, Not a Value

aspects.says: Boxing is tried before varargs, so a single int goes to an Object overload rather than a varargs one.
basis: section:Widening First, Then Boxing, Then Varargs: the First Phase That Fits Wins
aspects.reason: the same phase order the json-values practice and the quiz's widening question check; a separate varargs case would grade the order again, not a new idea

aspects.says: A char argument widens to an int or long overload in the first phase, before any other overload is considered.
basis: section:Widening First, Then Boxing, Then Varargs: the First Phase That Fits Wins

aspects.says: The compiler chooses an overload from the declared types of the arguments, so an argument held as Object reaches the Object overload whatever its class at run time.
basis: section:The Compiler Chooses an Overload From the Arguments' Declared Types
section:Spot the Problem: an equals That Works Until a Collection Calls It

aspects.says: Overloads must differ in their erased parameter types; neither the return type nor type arguments distinguish them.
basis: section:Overloads Must Differ in Erased Parameter Types: the Return Type and Type Arguments Don't Count

aspects.says: On a List<Integer>, remove with an int argument removes by index; removing a value needs an Integer argument.
basis: section:On a List of Integers, remove(int) Takes an Index, Not a Value

aspects.says: A subclass method with a narrower parameter type is an overload, not an override, so a call through the parent's type still runs the parent's method.
basis: section:The Compiler Chooses an Overload From the Arguments' Declared Types
section:Spot the Problem: an equals That Works Until a Collection Calls It

aspects.says: A null argument goes to the most specific overload, and when two unrelated overloads fit the call doesn't compile, so adding an overload can break callers' builds.
basis: section:null Goes to the Most Specific Overload, and Two Unrelated Ones Don't Compile

aspects.says: Widening is tried before boxing, so a long argument goes to a double overload rather than a Long one.
basis: section:Widening First, Then Boxing, Then Varargs: the First Phase That Fits Wins
